prompt: Which part of a home-made backup script does the lesson single out as the one people get wrong?
hint: It shows up months later, as a recovery that stops.

choices.text: Compressing the files before they are copied
choices.why: Compression is easy to add and easy to see working; its absence costs space, not data.

choices.text: Running pg_basebackup with the right options every night
choices.why: That part is one command and fails loudly when it fails.

choices.text: Deleting old log that kept backups still need
choices.why: Right. Retention has to know which segments each kept backup depends on; deleting by age leaves a gap nobody sees.

choices.text: Choosing a name for the directory the backups are kept in
choices.why: Nothing depends on the name.

prompt: With pgBackRest taking and verifying the backups, what is still true?
hint: Lesson 1.

choices.text: A backup is a claim until it is restored
choices.why: Right. The tool makes better copies; only a restore says they work.

choices.text: Restoring is no longer necessary, because every file is checksummed and checked
choices.why: A checksum proves the bytes did not change, not that a server starts on them or that the data is right.

choices.text: Retention has to be done by hand with find and rm
choices.why: pgBackRest's expire does retention, with its dependencies.

choices.text: The archive_command from lesson 4 has to stay as it was
choices.why: pgBackRest replaces it with archive-push.

prompt: Match each pgBackRest word with what it means.
hint: One is a place, one is a server's backups inside it.

pairs.right: Where backups and archived log are kept
One server's backups, under a name you choose
The command archive_command runs for each segment
Proves a segment travels from the server to the repository

right_distractors: The copy of the data directory a restore starts from

prompt: Why does every pgBackRest command in the lesson start with `sudo -u postgres`?
hint: Who owns the data directory?

choices.text: pgBackRest refuses to run for anyone with a password
choices.why: There is no such rule.

choices.text: The repository is on another machine that only knows postgres
choices.why: The repository is a local directory here.

choices.text: ana is not allowed to connect to the database
choices.why: ana is a superuser; the restriction is about files, not connections.

choices.text: It has to read the data directory, which postgres owns
choices.why: Right. pgBackRest runs as the user the server's files belong to.

prompt: What does `pgbackrest check` prove that `stanza-create` does not?
hint: It waits for something to arrive.

choices.text: That the configuration file has no typing mistakes in it
choices.why: A typing mistake would usually fail stanza-create too; check proves more than parsing.

choices.text: That archiving works end to end
choices.why: Right: a segment switched on the server reaches the repository through archive_command.

choices.text: That every backup in the repository can be restored
choices.why: check takes no backup and restores nothing.

choices.text: That the server has data checksums enabled
choices.why: It does not test that.

prompt: What does an incremental copy that a differential does not?
hint: Since when?

choices.text: Everything, like a full
choices.why: That is a full backup.

choices.text: What changed since any last backup
choices.why: Right. A differential copies everything changed since the last full.

choices.text: Only the write-ahead log
choices.why: Both copy data files; the log is archived continuously anyway.

choices.text: Rows inserted, but not rows updated
choices.why: pgBackRest works on files; it knows nothing about rows.

prompt: One new order made the incremental backup copy 4.5 MB. Why so much for one row?
hint: By default, what is the unit pgBackRest compares?

choices.text: Every incremental copies at least one full segment of log
choices.why: Segments are archived separately; the 4.5 MB is data files.

choices.text: Compression was switched off for the incremental
choices.why: The repository size was 817.9 KB; it was compressed.

choices.text: The incremental copied the differential's files again
choices.why: It refers to them; it does not copy them again.

choices.text: A changed file is copied whole
choices.why: Right. The row went into the orders file, and without repo-block the unit is the file, so one changed row copies the 3 MB table and its indexes.

prompt: To restore an incremental taken on Thursday, what has to be intact?
hint: Read its backup reference list.

choices.text: The full, every backup between, and the incremental
choices.why: Right. Every link in the chain is one more thing that has to be intact.

choices.text: The incremental alone
choices.why: An incremental holds only what changed; the rest comes from the backups it refers to.

choices.text: The incremental and the last full
choices.why: That is enough for a differential. An incremental also needs whatever it was taken after.

choices.text: Every backup in the repository
choices.why: Only the chain it refers to; other fulls are irrelevant to it.

prompt: Order the three kinds of backup from the one that copies most to the one that copies least, for a database changed a little every day and backed up daily.
hint: Each copies what changed since a different point.
trap: A full copies everything; a differential everything since the full, which grows through the week; an incremental only since yesterday's backup.

prompt: With `repo1-retention-full=2`, a third full backup finished. What did `expire` remove?
hint: It works in sets.

choices.text: Only the oldest full backup's files
choices.why: Its differential and incremental depended on it and went with it.

choices.text: Archived segments older than a week
choices.why: pgBackRest decides by dependency, not by age.

choices.text: That full's whole set, and its log
choices.why: Right: the oldest full, the backups that depended on it, then the segments no remaining backup needs.

choices.text: Nothing, because three is within two fulls plus a margin
choices.why: There is no margin: two means two.

prompt: A team's own script deletes archived segments older than seven days, and keeps two weekly full backups. What breaks?
hint: How old is the older full on Saturday?

choices.text: No harm: seven days of log covers a weekly backup
choices.why: The older full is up to fourteen days old, and it needs every segment since its start.

choices.text: The newer full cannot be restored at all
choices.why: The newer full's log is recent and is kept.

choices.text: The repository runs out of space
choices.why: It deletes more, not less.

choices.text: A recovery that stops at a silent gap
choices.why: Right. Recovery from the older full stops at the gap, and nothing reports it: the backup is kept and its log is not, which is the failure retention-by-dependency avoids.

prompt: Fulls are taken every Sunday and two are kept. On Saturday evening, about how many days ago is the oldest moment you can restore?
hint: Last Sunday's full and the one before.

prompt: In pgBackRest 2.50, what exit status does `verify` give when it finds a damaged file?
hint: The capture ran echo $? after it.

choices.text: 1, like any failing command
choices.why: That is what one would expect, and it is not what it does.

choices.text: 2, meaning a warning
choices.why: It printed 0.
Right. It exits with 0 whatever it finds; only the report says what happened.

choices.text: It does not exit until the damage is repaired
choices.why: It finished in under a second.

prompt: A job runs `pgbackrest verify --output=text` and treats empty output as success. Why is that wrong?
hint: Look at what the plain verify printed on a healthy repository and on a damaged one.

choices.text: It makes silence the pass, and a pass has to be something said
choices.why: Right. The job accepts only the line status: ok from the full report; anything else, silence included, is a failure.

choices.text: Empty output means verify did not run
choices.why: It ran; it simply prints nothing without --verbose when all is well.

choices.text: A job is never allowed to read a command's output
choices.why: Reading the report is exactly the fix.

choices.text: --output=text is not a valid option
choices.why: It is valid; it just is not enough without --verbose.

prompt: How many files did `verify` check in each full backup?
hint: total files checked.

prompt: A backup fails verification. What does the lesson do with it?
hint: Can a checksum mismatch be repaired?

choices.text: Repairs the file from the live server
choices.why: The file is the server's state at backup time; the live server's is a different moment.

choices.text: Removes it with expire --set and takes a new full
choices.why: Right. A failing backup cannot be fixed, only replaced.

choices.text: Leaves it, because the other full is still valid
choices.why: A known-bad backup in the repository is one somebody may restore from.

choices.text: Runs verify again until it passes
choices.why: The damage does not go away by asking again.

prompt: A restore test is made without `--archive-mode=off`, on a server whose `archive_command` pushes to the same stanza. What goes wrong?
hint: The copy carries the original's settings.

choices.text: The restore refuses to start
choices.why: It starts; that is the problem.

choices.text: The live server stops archiving
choices.why: It carries on, and its archive is now mixed with the copy's.

choices.text: Two histories end up in one archive
choices.why: Right. The copy pushes its own log into the live server's stanza, from a different history: two servers' log under one name, and the next recovery could replay the wrong one.

choices.text: Nothing, because the copy has a different port
choices.why: The stanza is chosen by archive_command, not by the port.

prompt: What does `restore_command`, written by pgBackRest into the restored copy, do?
hint: It is the reverse of archive_command.

choices.text: Fetches archived segments from the repository when recovery asks
choices.why: Right. That is what lets the copy replay past the end of the backup.

choices.text: Restores the copy again every time the server starts
choices.why: It runs only during recovery, one segment at a time.

choices.text: Pushes the copy's segments back to the repository
choices.why: That would be archive_command, and it was turned off.

choices.text: Checks the copy against the live server
choices.why: Nothing in recovery compares with the live server; the report did that.

prompt: The nightly job is in the postgres crontab and exits with 1 when verify fails. What is still missing?
hint: What if the job stops running at all?

choices.text: A second crontab line to run it twice
choices.why: Running it twice does not tell anybody it failed.

choices.text: set -x, so every command is printed
choices.why: Printing commands helps debugging, not noticing.

choices.text: A --type=full on every run
choices.why: That changes cost, not whether anybody notices failures.

choices.text: Something that alerts on a failure, and on a night with no run
choices.why: Right. On a machine with no mail set up, cron's output goes nowhere.

prompt: The nightly script counts the verify as a pass only if the report contains the exact line `status: ___`.
hint: Two letters.

prompt: The newest full backup has one damaged file, and two incrementals were taken after it. What does the full verify report say about them?
hint: What does an incremental take from its full?

choices.text: They are valid, because their own files are intact
choices.why: They refer to the damaged file in the full; a restore from them would use it.

choices.text: They are invalid too
choices.why: Right. The job's report listed the full and both incrementals as invalid: one damaged file, three unusable backups.

choices.text: They are not checked, because verify only reads fulls
choices.why: It checked all of them.

choices.text: They are deleted automatically by expire
choices.why: Nothing is deleted until somebody decides to.

prompt: A database changes heavily all day. Which rhythm keeps restores depending on few backups while keeping nightly copies small?
hint: Count what a Friday restore needs in each case.

choices.text: One full a month and an incremental each night
choices.why: A restore late in the month needs the full and up to thirty incrementals, all intact.

choices.text: A full weekly and a differential nightly
choices.why: Right. Any night's restore needs exactly two backups.

choices.text: Only incrementals, after a single first full
choices.why: The chain grows for ever, and so does what a restore depends on.

choices.text: A full every night and nothing else
choices.why: That keeps restores simple and makes every nightly copy as big as the database.
